claims.text: TCP moves bytes between two ports only after both ends have set up a connection; while that connection lasts, every byte arrives once, in the order it was sent.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 2.2 — TCP provides a reliable, in-order, byte-stream service; section 3.5.2 for a connection ending under bytes still in flight

claims.text: A connection exists as state remembered at both ends, not as something the network holds, and it normally lasts until each side has said it is finished.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 3.3.1 (Transmission Control Block is per-connection state at each end); section 3.6 (CLOSE is simplex); RFC 791 section 1.4 (IP has no connections)

claims.text: Setting up a TCP connection takes three short messages: one side offers, the other accepts and offers back, the first accepts in turn.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 3.5 — the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)

claims.text: The network carries each packet on its own and may lose it, deliver a copy of it, or deliver it out of the order it was sent.
claims.source_hint: RFC 791 section 1.4 — each datagram is an independent entity, no acknowledgments, no retransmissions; RFC 768 for duplicates

claims.text: UDP sends each packet on its own with no connection set up beforehand and no promise that the packet arrives, arrives once, or arrives in turn.
claims.source_hint: RFC 768 — the protocol is transaction oriented, delivery and duplicate protection are not guaranteed

claims.text: Your data waits only for the other side's answer, message 2: message 3 needs no answer of its own, so your data follows it straight away and the wait is one trip out and back.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 3.5, text after Figure 6 — the ACK in line 4 needs no reply and data follows in line 5

claims.text: Each side of a connection remembers four numbers — its own address and port, and the other side's address and port — and that set of four is what names the connection.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 3.4.1 (a connection is defined by a pair of sockets) and 3.3.1 (the TCB holds local and remote addresses and ports)

claims.text: One listening port serves many connections at the same time: two connections from the same machine to 8080 differ at least in the asking side's port, so no two carry the same four numbers, and two programs asking for 8080 at once do not wait for each other.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 3.4.1; RFC 9112 section 9 — servers maintain thousands of concurrent connections (refs/rfc/rfc9112.txt lines 1296-1304)

claims.text: TCP numbers every lump of bytes it sends; the receiving side puts them back in order and says which ones it has, and the sending side sends again anything it does not hear about.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 2.2 (loss detected via sequence numbers), 3.8 (the sender tracks the oldest unacknowledged number and retransmits)

claims.text: UDP numbers nothing and sends nothing again, and UDP itself does not tell the sending side that a packet was lost.
claims.source_hint: RFC 768 — the UDP header carries no sequence number and the protocol defines no acknowledgement or retransmission; RFC 791 section 1.4

claims.text: The script asks for five connections in four checks; the first three end differently, and the last shows a listener taking a second connection as readily as the first. `nc -z` asks for a connection without sending data and prints a line only when it gets one; a failure shows only in its exit code.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/tcp-connect.txt at tag stage-0: an nc line appears only for the two successes; attempts 2 and 3 print only the script's own echo

claims.text: In the lab, `nc -z -w 3 localhost 8080` reaches Caddy and prints `Connection to localhost (::1) 8080 port [tcp/http-alt] succeeded!`; `[tcp/http-alt]` is only the name the lab box's own list of well-known ports gives 8080, and nothing the connection depends on.
claims.source_hint: Run `scripts/network/tcp-connect.sh` at tag stage-0; `/etc/services` in the lab box maps 8080/tcp to http-alt

claims.text: From inside the lab box, `nc -z -w 3 localhost 9999` gets a refusal (a reset) as the reply to message 1, in place of message 2, because the machine is up but holds nothing on that port; it is an answer, so the attempt ends at once, with exit code 1.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 3.5.2 — a segment for a connection that does not exist is answered with a reset; outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/tcp-connect.txt lines 5-6 and who-listens.txt

claims.text: `nc -z -w 3 203.0.113.1 80` gets no reply of any kind to message 1, so it ends only when the 3-second limit set by `-w 3` runs out (a timeout), with the same exit code 1 as the refusal; without that limit it would wait longer.
claims.source_hint: Run `scripts/network/tcp-connect.sh` at tag stage-0 and time attempt 3; `nc -h`: -w is the timeout for connects

claims.text: `203.0.113.1` lies in a range set aside for writing examples rather than for real machines.
claims.source_hint: RFC 5737 section 3 — 203.0.113.0/24 (TEST-NET-3) is reserved for use in documentation and should not appear on the public Internet

claims.text: Every command finishes with a number, 0 when it worked and something else when it did not, and `$?` prints it; joined with `&&`, the second command runs only when the first gave 0, and joined with `||`, only when it did not.
claims.source_hint: GNU Bash manual sections 3.2.3 (lists of commands) and 3.4.2 (`$?` holds the exit status of the most recent pipeline); outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/tcp-connect.txt

claims.text: `::1` is how a machine names itself in the newer, longer form of address, so a connection that reaches it never leaves the machine.
claims.source_hint: RFC 4291 section 2.5.3 — 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1, written `::1`, is the loopback address a node uses to send to itself

claims.text: HTTP as you meet it here travels over a TCP connection, so a page opened at `localhost:8080` needed the three handshake messages before anything else moved.
claims.source_hint: refs/rfc/rfc9112.txt section 9 (lines 1282-1294) — the `http` URI scheme indicates a default connection of TCP over IP

claims.text: Encryption is added on top of an established TCP connection rather than replacing the handshake that opened it.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 section 1 — TLS asks of the transport only a reliable, in-order stream, which the TCP connection must already provide

claims.text: A refusal is an answer saying nothing holds that port, so it tells you the machine is up; a timeout is the absence of any answer, so the address may be wrong or something in between is dropping packets.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 3.5.2 (a request for a port with no listener is answered with a reset); refs/kubernetes-website .../kubeadm/high-availability.md:149-155

claims.text: A name lookup goes out over UDP and asks a second time if nothing comes back, instead of setting up a connection to carry one short question.
claims.source_hint: RFC 1035 sections 4.2 and 4.2.1 — UDP on port 53 is the recommended method for standard queries, and lost queries require a retransmission strategy

claims.text: Leaving out the handshake and the sending-again is worth it when setting up a connection costs more than the question is worth and the asker can simply ask again, which is why a name lookup goes over UDP.
claims.source_hint: RFC 768 (applications wanting ordered reliable delivery should use TCP) and RFC 1035 section 4.2.1 (UDP recommended for standard queries, with retransmission)

claims.text: Closing a TCP connection is per direction: one side says it is finished, and the connection is closed only once the other side has said the same.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9293 section 3.6 — each side sends its own FIN and has it acknowledged; the peer stays half-closed until its own application closes

claims.text: The side that opens a connection normally leaves its own port number to the operating system, which hands the program a free one each time; a program can ask for a particular one, but few do.
claims.source_hint: RFC 6056 sections 1 and 2 — the client's port is normally left unspecified and chosen by the networking stack, though some applications bind a specific one; 51000 is in 49152-65535

claims.text: The second line of the quoted block re-runs `scripts/network/tcp-connect.sh` inside the lab box, so it runs the same way on any machine; a browser tab's `localhost:8080` on your own machine is passed on to the same Caddy in the lab.
claims.source_hint: don-hang@stage-0: tcp-connect.sh l.5 and lab-run.sh re-exec via `docker compose exec lab`; docker-compose.yml: lab publishes 8080:8080, web shares its network

beyond_scope: Says `203.0.113.1` sits in a range set aside for examples, so the third attempt's silence is not read as a broken lab.
Names `::1` as the newer, longer form of a machine's own address and `[tcp/http-alt]` as `nc`'s name for 8080, to explain a line the captured output prints.

Says in one sentence that every command finishes with a number, that `$?` prints it, and what `&&` and `||` do with it, so the transcript's `exit code 1` and both failure lines can be read (junior review, section 5).
